title: You are not a model. Don’t price per token. | Andreessen Horowitz
gist: a16z Growth partners argue that AI application companies destroy their own economics by inheriting the model layer's token meter, anchoring their price to a cost curve that keeps falling; they prescribe a three-tier ladder — tokens for raw model access, credits mapped to recognizable units of work for the middle of the stack, and outcome pricing where results are attributable — backed by a survey of 50 technical AI buyers in which 27 preferred credits versus 14 who preferred tokens, and by Clay's disclosure that it mispriced Pro-segment credits in 2022 and ran that segment at a loss for years.

themes.theme: Token pricing as an inherited defect

insights.claim: Token pricing was a rational metering choice only at the model layer, dating to OpenAI's 2020 API launch, and became a category error once ChatGPT's 2022 debut spawned applications that bundle proprietary data, tools, orchestration, integrations, and workflow logic on top of inference.
insights.speaker: Tugce Erten, Sarah Wang
insights.so_what: Treat an application-layer company still billing per token as carrying an unfixed pricing defect, not a neutral packaging choice, when underwriting its revenue quality.
insights.quote: Token pricing began in the right place: the model layer.
insights.locator: Token pricing began in the right place

insights.claim: An application that prices in tokens imports the model provider's cost structure into its own customer relationship and anchors its value to a unit whose cost keeps falling.
insights.speaker: Tugce Erten, Sarah Wang
insights.so_what: Falling inference prices become a revenue headwind rather than a margin tailwind for token-priced applications — a structural short signal on their pricing power.
insights.quote: it imports the model provider’s cost structure into the relationship with the customer and anchors the product’s value to a unit whose cost keeps falling
insights.locator: When an application prices that work in tokens

insights.claim: Token-based pricing trains customers to benchmark a specialized application against raw compute, giving away the value of data, workflow, and orchestration and potentially locking the vendor into weak margins.
insights.speaker: Tugce Erten, Sarah Wang
insights.so_what: The moat a company builds in data and orchestration is only monetizable if the meter doesn't invite a compute comparison — check the billing unit before believing the moat.
insights.locator: Getting this wrong is difficult to undo

insights.claim: Pricing architecture is close to irreversible once set, because a token-anchored customer expectation is difficult to unwind after the fact.
insights.speaker: Tugce Erten, Sarah Wang
insights.so_what: Pricing model is a durable, hard-to-repair attribute of an AI company — weight it like unit economics, not like a marketing variable that can be A/B tested later.
insights.quote: Getting this wrong is difficult to undo.
insights.locator: Getting this wrong is difficult to undo

insights.claim: Token pricing forces buyers to forecast context length, retrieval volume, retries, reasoning time, and output tokens, converting what should be a simple ROI calculation into a separate compute-forecasting exercise for every AI application a company deploys.
insights.speaker: Tugce Erten, Sarah Wang
insights.so_what: Unforecastable spend is a hidden sales-cycle tax; token-priced vendors should show longer procurement cycles and weaker net expansion than work-priced peers.
insights.locator: A support leader can estimate how many conversations

insights.claim: The governing rule proposed is to price at the highest layer of value a company can reliably measure, attribute, and defend — tokens for model access, a recognizable value unit (often credits) for useful work, and the outcome itself where a business result is clearly attributable.
insights.speaker: Tugce Erten, Sarah Wang
insights.so_what: A portable diligence test: ask which of the three layers a company actually sells and whether its meter matches — mismatch signals margin leakage.
insights.quote: we believe companies should price at the highest layer of value that they can reliably measure, attribute, and defend
insights.locator: Instead, we believe companies should price

insights.claim: The two ends of the AI stack have straightforward pricing while the difficult middle — where most AI applications actually sit — has no universal metric because each category packages value differently.
insights.speaker: Tugce Erten, Sarah Wang
insights.so_what: Expect pricing heterogeneity across AI app comps; cross-company revenue-quality comparisons on a single usage metric will be misleading.
insights.quote: The middle is harder. That’s where most AI applications live.
insights.locator: 1. Price the Layer You Sell

insights.claim: The correct pricing question is not what the AI pricing metric is but what unit of value the customer already understands and can be measured consistently.
insights.speaker: Tugce Erten, Sarah Wang
insights.so_what: Gives a one-question screen for evaluating any AI vendor's pricing narrative in diligence calls.
insights.quote: What unit of value does the customer already understand, and can we measure it consistently?
insights.locator: The right question is not

insights.claim: The unit of sale for AI applications should be the completed job — an account-research agent sells a completed account brief, a coding agent sells an implemented change, a data platform sells a completed query, pipeline, or agent run — not the underlying searches and model calls.
insights.speaker: Tugce Erten, Sarah Wang
insights.so_what: Vertical-by-vertical, the defensible billing unit is identifiable in advance; companies that have named theirs are further along the value-capture curve.
insights.locator: For example, an account-research agent

insights.claim: Pricing metrics are expected to migrate over a product's life: voice AI may begin with minutes and move toward conversations resolved, while copilots may begin with seats and add usage-based pricing as agentic work creates greater variation in cost and value.
insights.speaker: Tugce Erten, Sarah Wang
insights.so_what: Watch for meter migrations in voice AI and copilot vendors as a leading indicator of maturing value capture and potential step-changes in ARPU.
insights.locator: Voice AI may begin with minutes

insights.claim: Once an outcome becomes observable, attributable, and valuable enough to support a stable price, the meter should move again to price the result directly — a resolved support conversation, a qualified lead, a booked meeting, a processed claim, or a recovered dollar.
insights.speaker: Tugce Erten, Sarah Wang
insights.so_what: Outcome pricing is the endgame for the highest-attribution categories; those verticals should see the strongest pricing power and the widest gross-margin dispersion.
insights.locator: 5. Move to Outcomes When Value Is Clear

insights.claim: In a survey of 50 technical AI buyers, 27 preferred credits tied to recognizable work while only 14 preferred tokens.
insights.speaker: Tugce Erten, Sarah Wang
insights.so_what: Roughly a 2:1 buyer preference for work-based credits over tokens — demand-side evidence that the token default is a vendor habit, not a customer requirement.
insights.quote: In our survey of 50 technical AI buyers, 27 preferred credits tied to recognizable work, while only 14 preferred tokens.
insights.locator: In our survey of 50 technical AI buyers

insights.claim: When buyers ask about tokens they are actually asking for one of two things — comparability or the ability to allocate spend — and neither need requires tokens to be the commercial unit.
insights.speaker: Tugce Erten, Sarah Wang
insights.so_what: Vendor claims that customers demand token pricing are usually a misread of a reporting request — a signal of weak pricing discipline rather than genuine market constraint.
insights.locator: 2. Customers Want Legibility, Not Tokens

insights.claim: Token-based comparison across AI applications is false precision, because each application combines different models, data, tools, and levels of automation so a token flowing through one product does not produce the same work as a token flowing through another.
insights.speaker: Tugce Erten, Sarah Wang
insights.so_what: Undermines token-normalized benchmarking that buyers and analysts use to compare AI vendors; cost-per-token comparables should be discounted.
insights.quote: A token flowing through one product does not produce the same work as a token flowing through another.
insights.locator: First, buyers want a common benchmark

insights.claim: The recommended resolution is to expose enough underlying usage detail for trust and chargeback reporting without making that usage the commercial unit, because the billing meter and the underlying cost meter do not need to be the same.
insights.speaker: Tugce Erten, Sarah Wang
insights.so_what: Separating transparency from the meter is the practical unlock — a checkable product capability (usage reporting) that lets a vendor upgrade pricing without losing enterprise buyers.
insights.quote: Transparency does not require the billing meter and the underlying cost meter to be the same.
insights.locator: Transparency does not require the billing meter

themes.theme: Credit design: currency vs. value metric

insights.claim: Credits alone do not fix token pricing — a credit is a currency rather than a value metric, and a weak credit system that merely converts token counts into an opaque internal currency hides the meter without improving it.
insights.speaker: Tugce Erten, Sarah Wang
insights.so_what: Do not credit a company for 'moving to credits' — inspect what a credit actually buys, since cost-plus token credits carry the same margin exposure.
insights.quote: A weak credit system converts token counts into an opaque internal currency. It hides the meter without improving it.
insights.locator: 3. Credits Should Map Work to Value

insights.claim: Strong credit systems use a few intuitive effort bands where a small bug fix costs less than a multi-file feature, summarizing one contract clause costs less than reviewing the full agreement, and enriching one record costs less than a multi-step account research workflow.
insights.speaker: Tugce Erten, Sarah Wang
insights.so_what: Effort-banded credits are the concrete implementation pattern to look for when assessing whether an AI vendor's packaging is durable.
insights.locator: A strong credit system maps to work

insights.claim: The stated test of a credit system is comprehension: buyers usually know their workload before they know their compute load, and if customers cannot understand the credit system in a few sentences it is too complicated.
insights.speaker: Tugce Erten, Sarah Wang
insights.so_what: A fast qualitative screen usable in a single customer reference call — comprehension failure predicts pricing churn.
insights.quote: If customers cannot understand the credit system in a few sentences, it is too complicated.
insights.locator: The test is comprehension

insights.claim: Well-designed credits create commercial flexibility by letting one pool cover several workloads, agents, or automations while procurement manages a single contract.
insights.speaker: Tugce Erten, Sarah Wang
insights.so_what: A single credit pool is a land-and-expand mechanism — it lowers the friction of adding new agent workloads inside an existing contract.
insights.locator: Create commercial flexibility

themes.theme: Margin structure of AI apps vs. SaaS

insights.claim: AI applications break the traditional SaaS assumption of near-zero marginal cost per user, because every user can generate inference, retrieval, search, tool calls, third-party data, media generation, retries, and failed runs.
insights.speaker: Tugce Erten, Sarah Wang
insights.so_what: Apply a COGS-heavy mental model to AI app comps; SaaS-era gross-margin multiples are the wrong starting point.
insights.locator: In traditional SaaS, an additional user

insights.claim: Fast revenue growth can conceal a structurally weak AI business if each incremental dollar of revenue is quickly paid back to model, cloud, or data providers.
insights.speaker: Tugce Erten, Sarah Wang
insights.so_what: Growth rate alone is an unreliable quality signal in AI apps — underwrite incremental gross margin per dollar of new revenue instead.
insights.quote: Fast growth can hide a weak business if each new dollar of revenue is quickly paid back to model, cloud, or data providers.
insights.locator: 4. Credits Can Protect Margins

insights.claim: The prescribed margin architecture separates two decisions: customer value, willingness to pay, and competition set the price of the credit pool, while relative cost and complexity set how many credits each task consumes.
insights.speaker: Tugce Erten, Sarah Wang
insights.so_what: This decoupling is the specific mechanism that lets an AI app raise gross margin without repricing the customer — a concrete lever to check for in a company's pricing system.
insights.locator: The pricing system needs to separate two decisions

insights.claim: Decoupling the credit price from the credit cost preserves margin upside from model routing, caching, prompt optimization, better infrastructure, and a shifting mix of proprietary and open-source models, so that falling model costs can accrue partly to the application rather than being passed through in full.
insights.speaker: Tugce Erten, Sarah Wang
insights.so_what: Work-priced AI apps are structurally long the deflation in inference costs; token-priced ones are not — a key differentiator in forecasting gross-margin expansion.
insights.quote: if underlying model costs fall, the application may even be able to retain part of the benefit because customers are paying for work, not just reimbursing the company for compute
insights.locator: This separation enables the vendor to protect margin

themes.theme: Clay case study and hybrid meters

insights.claim: Clay disclosed in a 2026 pricing memo that it had mispriced credits in its Pro segment back in 2022 and operated that segment at a loss for years.
insights.speaker: Tugce Erten, Sarah Wang
insights.so_what: A named, dated example that credit mispricing can produce multi-year segment-level losses — evidence that pricing errors compound silently rather than surfacing quickly.
insights.locator: Clay offers a helpful example

insights.claim: Clay's revised model separates Data Credits for third-party data from Actions for orchestration work, keeps fixed pricing for models with predictable costs, and passes through the actual token cost of volatile and expensive reasoning models without a markup.
insights.speaker: Tugce Erten, Sarah Wang
insights.so_what: A replicable multi-meter blueprint: markup where costs are predictable, at-cost pass-through where they are volatile — the design pattern to look for in next-generation AI pricing.
insights.quote: Clay uses different meters for different layers: Actions for platform value and token pass-through for unpredictable model costs.
insights.locator: Clay offers a helpful example

insights.claim: Hybrid pricing is expected to become the norm — seats for access, credits for variable work, token pass-through for unusually expensive or unpredictable model calls, and outcome fees where attribution is clean — with the failure mode being the wrong meter on the wrong layer rather than the number of meters.
insights.speaker: Tugce Erten, Sarah Wang
insights.so_what: Expect AI app revenue to become multi-component and harder to model; single-metric ARR analysis will lose explanatory power.
insights.quote: Multiple meters are not the problem, but avoid using the wrong meter for the wrong layer.
insights.locator: Many products will use hybrids

insights.claim: Token pass-through remains legitimate but only as an explicit component of a hybrid model in highly competitive or technically sophisticated markets, particularly for unusually expensive or volatile model usage — never as the default expression of the product's value.
insights.speaker: Tugce Erten, Sarah Wang
insights.so_what: Distinguishes defensible pass-through from value-destroying token pricing when assessing a vendor's disclosed pricing page.
insights.locator: In highly competitive or technically sophisticated markets

insights.claim: Token pricing pulls the customer conversation toward a falling cost curve, which is a poor anchor for a product whose usefulness, reliability, and role in the workflow should keep rising.
insights.speaker: Tugce Erten, Sarah Wang
insights.so_what: Frames the core divergence to watch — application value trending up against inference cost trending down — and which meter lets a company capture the gap.
insights.quote: Token pricing pulls the customer conversation toward a cost curve that keeps falling.
insights.locator: Make Value Visible
